items.title: Russian strikes across Ukraine kill 3 people as Kyiv struggles to counter escalating attacks - AP News
items.summary: Russian strikes across Ukraine kill 3 people as Kyiv struggles to counter escalating attacks  AP News
items.content:
Image caption, Smoke billows from Yandex's Sasovo hub following a Ukrainian strike on Thursday
Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.
Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.
The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".
Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv , killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.
But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

Pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk arrested in Montenegro
Founder of influential Rybar blog detained after warnings of attempts to destabilise Balkan country, officials say
A leading pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger with reported ties to Russia’s intelligence services has been arrested in Montenegro , after warnings of attempts to destabilise the Balkan country, officials have said.
Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Rybar war blog, was detained on Friday alongside his wife and three other Russians by police and security agents in the Adriatic resort town of Risan, on suspicion of spreading Russian influence, local media reported.
Montenegro’s prime minister, Milojko Spajić, confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X, saying it followed warnings that the country would face attempts at destabilisation and hybrid warfare.
The Montenegrin news outlet Vijesti reported later on Friday that Zvinchuk and the other detainees were to be expelled from the country on national security grounds.
The Russian Telegram news channel Baza said officers detained Zvinchuk at the luxury Mövenpick hotel in Risan. It said the group was taken to Podgorica, Montenegro’s capital, for questioning and their phones and passports were confiscated.
Founded in 2018 by Zvinchuk, a former press officer at Russia’s defence ministry, Rybar is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine , with more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram. It forms part of a sprawling online media ecosystem that promotes Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
But Rybar’s activities extend well beyond Ukraine, with the channel promoting pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East. More recently, it has been accused of amplifying far-right narratives surrounding the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in north Africa.
“At the moment, the project team is in contact with Russia’s foreign ministry, which is working to resolve the situation. Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released,” the channel said on Telegram.
Milojko Spajić, Montenegro’s prime minister, said the arrest followed warnings of attempts to destabilise his country and hybrid warfare. Photograph: Boris Pejovic/EPA Britain sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar in December 2025 over their role in spreading Kremlin propaganda and undermining support for Ukraine. The British government said Zvinchuk received funding from the Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec, and worked with members of Russia’s intelligence services.
The US has separately accused Zvinchuk of attempting to interfere in the 2024 presidential election, offering a reward of up to $10m for information about those involved.
Days before his arrest, Zvinchuk boasted on social media that he had managed to enter Montenegro despite being subject to western sanctions and an entry ban. He mocked a border guard who, he said, had searched his belongings but failed to check his name against a database.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow was aware of Zvinchuk’s detention and would work to secure his release.
Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev suggested Moscow could detain European and American citizens to use in prisoner exchanges to secure Zvinchuk’s release. “We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots in order to get our own people back,” he wrote on social media.
The arrest is likely to further strain relations between Montenegro and Russia, which have long been tense. In 2016, Montenegrin authorities accused Russian operatives of plotting with Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup , allegations Moscow denied.
Montenegro, which joined Nato in 2017 and is seeking membership of the EU , imposed sanctions on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The country recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens from 1 November, closing off a popular holiday destination for Russian tourists as it brings its visa policy into line with the EU.

Putin relayed Iran war proposal to Trump, Kremlin says
Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's view on a possible resolution of the Iran conflict to U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian state media reported.
The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Trump said Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement Trump said he agreed with Putin.
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska.
Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's vision for a possible end to the war in Iran to U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian state media reported Saturday.
The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin sent the message to Trump "in agreement with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian," according to a Google translation.
Other Russian media reports said Putin spoke to Trump by  phone  after the Russian leader met Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan.
Interfax didn't elaborate on the specifics of how Iran sees the war — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets — coming to an end.
The White House didn't immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request to confirm the reported conversation between Putin and Trump.
Trump said Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement the U.S. president said he agreed with Putin during a phone call.
Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately thereafter, Trump said in a post on Truth Social . Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said.
The Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027 under a general license issued Friday.
Brent crude oil price, U.S. dollars per barrel, year to date
Iran has stepped up its attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with vessels coming under fire almost daily as Tehran tries to choke off a rebound in crude exports.
A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard official said Wednesday that Iran will block all "illicit routes" through Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency , an outlet considered close to the Guard.
The surge in attacks on tankers comes as crude oil exports from the Middle East rebounded in September to prewar levels, largely because the U.S. military escorted ships through Hormuz along Oman's coast.
An interim deal signed in June between the U.S. and Iran to pause hostilities to allow for negotiations quickly broke down.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately condemned Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Ukraine's leader warned that easing sanctions without a commitment from Russia to de-escalate the war will only prolong it.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in a social media post . "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
Diesel prices have surged worldwide as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries, forcing Moscow to ban diesel exports to global markets. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, further constraining fuel supplies.
Trump is under growing political pressure to lower fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Republicans face competitive elections in conservative strongholds like Iowa, where farmers feel the pinch of high diesel prices.

As the war in Iran pushes energy security ever higher on government agendas, importing countries want to diversify their sources of oil and gas. For IOCs and NOCs scanning the globe for upstream investments, resource holding countries are in pole position. Geopolitically stable contenders in the Caspian region include Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. These producers have a great opportunity to collaborate and elevate the region to play a bigger role as a reliable supplier of energy and natural resources.
Malcolm Forbes-Cable and Ian Simm from our Consulting team have spearheaded WoodMac's engagement in the region, along with Craig Saunders from Upstream Research and, on occasion, me. They shared their thoughts on the prospects for future regional autonomy.
Azerbaijan's strategic position to access global markets.
Azerbaijan not only ranks as a sizeable oil and gas producer in global terms but, importantly, is ahead of the game having invested in critical infrastructure to export its oil and gas from the landlocked Caspian Sea. Its upstream industry, more than a century old, rose to global significance early this millennium with the development of BP's giant offshore ACG and Shah Deniz projects.
These fields propelled total production to 1.2 million boe/d by 2010, with 80% of that oil. Output has held this level ever since, and on our forecasts will stay there through to the late 2030s helped by Phase 2 of TotalEnergies' Absheron gas project which FID'd last month. Gas has become the growth story, comprising about 60% of production in 2026.
The NOC SOCAR is a significant investor in all upstream projects. The government is also aiming to attract more investment offshore as well as onshore where ExxonMobil has a licence to explore a large unproven shale play. Azerbaijan's refining capacity is focused on meeting domestic fuel demand.
The construction of major export pipelines opened the 'Southern Corridor,' connecting Azerbaijan's oil and gas supplies to wider markets beyond the Caspian. The 1.2 million b/d BTC oil pipeline (2005) transports mainly Azerbaijani crude to the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan. Even topped up with volumes shipped across the Caspian from Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, BTC is substantially underutilised. The TANAP (2018) and TAP (2020) gas pipelines carry Azerbaijani gas through Georgia and Turkey and on to the European gas network via Greece and Italy.
New pipeline connectivity – the 'Middle Corridor'
Energy connectivity and diversification of export routes were big themes last week at the KIOGE conference in Almaty, Kazakhstan. A possible East-West 'Green Corridor' linking renewable power supply to Azerbaijan via an interconnector across the Caspian Sea was much discussed.
It is future oil and gas connectivity, however, that could be game changing for the region. NOC KazMunaiGas is the biggest resource holder in Kazakhstan, but the scale of resources has attracted IOC investors for decades. Key players include Chevron, ExxonMobil, Eni, Shell, TotalEnergies, CNPC, Lukoil and Inpex. Kazakhstan currently produces 2.2 million b/d of liquids, with over 1.5 million b/d exported through the CPC pipeline to a port near Novorossiysk on Russia's Black Sea coast. Flows have, however, been seriously disrupted by attacks on the pipeline and port facilities related to the Russia/Ukraine war. There is potential to lift export volumes by more than 0.2 million b/d if the next phase of the giant Kashagan project goes ahead.
Turkmenistan's situation as a substantial gas producer is different. The giant Galkynysh is the second largest gas field in the world, with exports contributing up to a third of the country's GDP. The exports, 34Bcm/year sold exclusively to China, are well below half of Qatar's larger North field gas exports in 2025. While the two countries have discussed additional sales there's been little progress. Turkmenistan needs to cultivate alternative export options if it is to commercialise Galkynysh's vast reserves. The main gas producers in Turkmenistan are NOC Turkmengaz, CNPC, Petronas and XRG.
A logical solution for the region is obvious – build new pipelines across the Caspian Sea to link Kazakhstan's oil and Turkmenistan's gas to the existing export routes through Azerbaijan to the Mediterranean and European gas network respectively. Filling in the missing links, cross-Caspian oil and gas pipelines, would complete the 'Middle Corridor,' a new Silk Road for molecules.
The Middle Corridor would give Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan the export optionality they seek, allow them to accelerate investment in their resource, and boost the availability of supply and energy security importing countries need. Azerbaijan, meanwhile, would capture valuable tariff revenues, and strengthen its position as a strategic linchpin all along the corridor.
Realisation of the concept is far from straight forward. Progress awaits answers to big questions, these three among them. How to gain support from multiple governments with varied, individual and vested interests, not only Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan but others not least Russia and China? Is Europe keen to commit to long-term gas contracts? And who finances the large-scale cross-border infrastructure – governments or the oil and gas industry?
The Caspian – an emerging source of critical minerals
Beyond oil and gas the Central Asian countries are rich in critical minerals. Efforts to attract foreign investment are ramping up as countries focus on developing their mining and processing industries to capitalise on the current dash for these vital resources. China's insatiable appetite is an obvious market but the pull from the west has also surged with the recognition of the strategic importance of these resources.

items.title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings
items.summary: Tsunami warnings are issued for neighbouring countries as videos of destruction circulate online.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Moment part of building collapses during Panama earthquake
A massive magnitude 7.7 earthquake has hit Panama, damaging buildings and causing widespread shaking.
About 4.6 million people felt moderate to severe tremors as a result of the quake, according to the US Geological Survey, which has said that the effects of the quake were "likely to be widespread".
It struck just before 15:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Friday, with an epicentre about 6.2 miles (10km) from the town of Pitaloza Arriba in south-central Panama.
Footage shared online appears to show collapsed buildings in the towns of Penonomé and Soná, including one of a man calling out to anyone trapped under the rubble of a collapsed building. No casualties have so far been reported.
Image caption, A maternity ward in Panama City was among the buildings evacuated during the tremors
Verified footage shows one side of a cathedral in Penonomé collapsed due to the shaking, as well as one of its spires.
Another video showed a local hotel had almost completely collapsed.
Ricardo Brown, who lives in the southern Herrera province, told news agency Reuters that the earthquake had damaged several homes in his neighbourhood of Las Minas.
"We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked and we're afraid it could fall on us," the 74-year-old said.
The full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, though several large aftershocks were also reported near the initial earthquake, potentially complicating the situation on the surface.
The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.
Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km from the epicentre, and were seen taking to the streets or sitting in nearby parks until the shaking had ceased.
Damage in the capital appears to be limited to that caused by debris falling from roofs.
Panama's President José Raúl Mulino said his entire government was mobilising in response to the earthquake, adding: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder."
Tsunami warnings were initially issued for 11 countries neighbouring Panama, before the US Tsunami Warning System confirmed there was no threat.
The Panama Canal - a vital waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans - was unaffected by the earthquake, the authority that oversees marine traffic through it said.
The earthquake comes just three days before Panama was scheduled to hold a national evacuation drill for dealing with a major earthquake.
It also follows devastating earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela earlier this year.

Trump appoints committee to investigate statements by the Fed’s Lisa Cook
President Donald Trump formally established a "committee of inquiry" to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook made false statements related to "one or more mortgage instruments," the White House announced Friday.
The extraordinary announcement is the latest development in Trump's long-running effort to fire Cook, a nominee of former President Joe Biden , from the central bank's board. Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, recently said the failure to do so by his handpicked chair, Kevin Warsh , is the fault of a "hostile" board.
The committee comprises three executive branch officials, including Kevin Hassett , Trump's top economic aide and a chief defender of the administration's economic record, according to a presidential memorandum posted on the White House website and shared Friday on social media.
The other two members are Keith Sonderling, Labor secretary and acting head of the Office of Government Ethics, and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Chair Andrea Lucas, according to the notice, which is dated Wednesday. No outside, independent arbiters are mentioned.
The highly unusual move, which hasn't been used in nearly a century, is bound to fuel new accusations that Trump and his aides are eroding the Fed's long-maintained independence while once again wielding government power against the president's enemies. Congressional Democrats quickly slammed the announcement, while Cook's lawyers expressed deep skepticism about the panel's validity.
There is no modern precedent for such a committee, though past presidents have convened similar panels. President William Taft in 1912 appointed a committee to investigate the Board of United States General Appraisers, and President Herbert Hoover did the same in 1931 to probe statements by the president of the Navy League.
The Supreme Court, in its June ruling temporarily blocking Trump from his first attempt to fire Cook, cited Taft's committee.
Trump's panel and Cook are scheduled to appear for an in-person hearing at the White House on Nov. 5, two days after the midterm election, the memo states. Its members can consult with the Department of Justice and other agencies "to aid in its inquiry," the notice says.
Cook's attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, sharply questioned the legitimacy of the inquiry, but nevertheless said the governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
"In light of the President's repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook – regardless of the facts and evidence — we have grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law," the lawyers told CNBC in a statement.
"But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board," they said.
"We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise. Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her," Lowell and Eisen said.
Trump first tried to fire Cook last year, after administration officials raised allegations that she made false statements on at least one mortgage-related document.
Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing and filed a lawsuit to block her dismissal. A federal court temporarily barred Trump from firing her, and the Supreme Court in June narrowly upheld that ruling.
But the high court did not stop Trump from trying again for Cook's removal. Rather, it rejected Trump's first bid because Cook was not given proper legal due process, and said any new attempt to fire her would require additional steps. Under the Federal Reserve Act, a president can remove a Fed governor only "for cause."
Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know
Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election
Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more'
In August, White House aide Dan Scavino told Cook in a letter that Trump was once again "considering" firing her in connection with the mortgage allegations.
"As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law," Trump states in the memo establishing the committee of inquiry, which is addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche.
"To assist me in carrying out that responsibility, the Committee shall investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is 'cause' for Governor Cook's removal" within the meaning identified by the Supreme Court, it says.
The Fed did not provide a comment and referred CNBC to Cook's lawyers.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., in a statement later Friday morning accused Trump of "convening an illegitimate show trial in his dangerous quest to illegally take over our nation's central bank."
"Instead of playing judge in a kangaroo court of his own making, Trump should end the war in Iran and cancel his chaotic tariffs," said Warren, the top-ranking Democrat on the Senate's Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said Trump "is escalating his smear campaign against Lisa Cook while turning the presidency into a personal ATM: crypto schemes, taxpayer-funded propaganda ads, cash for his family — the list could go on forever."
"This has nothing to do with 'ethical concerns.' It's about Trump trying to seize control of the Fed, something that would mean even more economic chaos for American families," Schumer said in an X post .

items.title: Eritrean troops in Ethiopia raise fears of a regional war
items.summary: Ethiopia and Eritrea are trading blame for confrontations in Tigray amid international calls for restraint. Their respective allies have the potential to catapult the conflict into a regional war.
items.content:
ENDF patrol on October 7: The airport of Mekelle is under Ethiopian government control. But witnesses have reported Eritrean troops towards Tigray's northern border. Image: REUTERS Advertisement
Various sources have confirmed the presence of  Eritrean armed forces in Ethiopia . An AFP report quoted a foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, as estimating that 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in the northenmost state of Ethiopia, Tigray.  
Meanwhile, Ethiopia and Eritrea have ramped up their war talk.
According to Reuters, the government of Ethiopia has written to the UN Security Council, calling for the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean troops from its territory.
In the letter, dated ‌Oct. 8, Ethiopian ‌Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia left "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea,"
in a post on X on October 7, Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Meskel had accused Ethiopia of "incessantly beating the drums of war."
Two days later, he wrote in Tigrinya, a working language of Eritrea and the main language of Tigray, that "the sovereign state of Eritrea is bound by blood and law." adding "woe to those who touch it."
This comes as  the regional conflict in Tigray has deteriorated rapidly in recent weeks.
Some experts have suggested that Ethiopia may have intentionally triggered the escalation. Just last week, it expelled diplomats from Egypt and Eritrea, causing the latter to sever diplomatic ties altogether.
On Monday, when Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five years as Ethiopian prime minister , he stated that access to the sea was a priority. The statement fueled fresh speculation that he intends to take Eritrea's strategic port of Assab by force and prompted fierce reactions from the Eritrean side.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Abiy's internal opposition: Tsimdo and the Alliance for Survival
While the Ethiopian National Defence Forces (ENDF), aided by the Tigray Peace Force milita, have made significant advances and notably recaptured the Tigray federal state capital of Mekelle , opposition to Ethiopia has found new formats for collaboration.
One is the Tsimdo movement, named after a Tigrinya term that loosely translates as "engagement."
"The Tsimdo concept initially surfaced through cross-border peace initiatives involving activists, religious figures, and local communities in the Tigray and Eritrea border villages in 2025," Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst with the US-based conflict monitor ACLED, told DW.
It has since undergone several reconfigurations and now encompasses diverse groups within Ethiopia, mostly defined along ethnic lines and with long-standing grievances against the federal government.
The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, or simply Alliance for Survival, that was proclaimed in September, stems from this movement. According to Jalale, the alliance aims at removing the current government and initiating a constitutional dialogue.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The new alliance says a lot about the long history of unresolved conflict in Ethiopia, said Abdurahman Sayed, an analyst at the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration.
"The fighting inside Ethiopia has never stopped," Sayed told DW.
"With the Oromo Liberation Army, it's been going on for decades, with the Amhara, it's been going on for the last three years, at least. With the Tigrayans, the Pretoria agreement about three years ago was just a cessation of hostility that would have led to some kind of sustainable peace by addressing the root causes of the conflict — but it failed to do that, so they're back to the conflict situation now."
However, of the seven groups in the alliance, ACLED data shows that only three were involved in recent fighting: The Tigrayan Defence Forces (TDF), the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), and a fairly recently formed ethnic Afar group called Ugugumo.
Amhara Fano fighters (pictured here in 2021) who fought in the two-year Tigray War are part of the new Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival Image: Solan Kolli/AFP
Joint declaration by Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia
The success of the Alliance for Survival would depend in large part on the support they get through external actors, according to ACLED. Those could include neighboring  Sudan , Egypt , Eritrea, and Somalia .
"All these four countries have grievances against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government," Sayed said.
"The Egyptians have issues with the Nile River and how it should be administered, including the dams that are already there and those planned to be built around the Nile River. The Sudanese also have their own concerns that Ethiopians are supporting the [Rapid Support Forces] militia , which is fighting the Sudanese army."
In the case of Somalia, the issue of sea access has sparked tensions. Landlocked Ethiopia has negotiated access to the port of Berbera in  Somaliland  . In 2024, it signed a memorandum of understanding with the breakaway region, causing uproar in Somalia , which considers the deal a violation of its national sovereignty. Turkish mediation was needed to calm things down.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"So all those neighboring countries have their own concerns and they feel this threat that is coming from Ethiopia needs to be tackled collectively."
On October 4, the leaders of the four countries issued  a joint declaration that didn't mention Ethiopia but seemed to send a strong signal. The leaders stressed the importance of international law, "particularly respect for the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the states of the region."
And they maintained that "the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states."
Although the leaders of Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia vowed to promote "peaceful solutions to conflicts," the reality on the ground may prove otherwise.

items.title: Trump created a committee to dig into the Fed's Lisa Cook. What is it and what comes next?
items.summary: Trump’s bid to fire the Fed's Lisa Cook follows a Supreme Court ruling and could affect Jerome Powell, central bank independence and interest rates.
items.content:
Trump’s Fed Lisa Cook committee explained: What happens next
President Donald Trump created a three-person committee to recommend whether he has cause to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook over mortgage fraud allegations she denies.
Cook is expected to appear before the committee Nov. 5, though questions remain about her legal exposure and whether the process is sufficiently independent.
The committee cannot fire Cook itself. Trump would make the final decision, which would likely trigger another court fight.
Federal Reserve Board Governor Lisa Cook speaks on "The Outlook for the Economy and Monetary Policy" at the Brookings Institution in Washington, D.C., U.S., November 3, 2025.
President Donald Trump on Friday announced an unusual legal step: He created a committee to help him decide whether to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook .
Trump has accused Cook of mortgage fraud , and in 2025 ordered her to be fired . The Supreme Court blocked that effort on procedural grounds but said he could try again. Trump in August informed Cook that he was considering another attempt to fire her. Her attorneys responded later that month, denying the allegations of fraud and saying Trump had no cause to remove her.
The decision to form what Trump is calling a "committee of inquiry" raises a number of questions about the path forward for Trump and Cook.
According to the president's memo , Cook is expected to attend a hearing at the White House on Nov. 5. She can bring an attorney. The committee will weigh the evidence against her and her response. She will have until Nov. 10 to follow up after the proceedings.
Then the committee will make a recommendation to the president as to whether there is cause to fire her from the Fed. The final call is up to the president. There is no set deadline for that final decision.
Trump appointed three people to hear the evidence against Cook: Kevin Hassett , director of the National Economic Council; Keith Sonderling , acting director of the Office of Government Ethics and Labor secretary; and Andrea R. Lucas , chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. All three are Trump appointees.
Yes, at least once. The Supreme Court's majority opinion in Trump v. Cook , written by Chief Justice John Roberts , mentions a precedent.
President William Howard Taft in 1912 convened a similar "committee of inquiry" to consider the removal of two members of the Board of General Appraisers, a precursor to what is now the U.S. Court of International Trade. The committee ultimately recommended their removal. Roberts describes the committee as "a prime example of the view that Taft was our 'most judicial president,' as he was our most 'presidential chief justice.' "
But notably, the Supreme Court didn't require Trump or other presidents to follow that example. The court says Cook was entitled to notice of the president's decision, an explanation of the evidence, and an opportunity to present her defense. That process could take place entirely in writing, Roberts notes.
A Fed governor is not "entitled to an audience with the President or a full-blown judicial trial," Roberts writes.
Her attorneys Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen said in a statement she "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her." Still, they said they "have grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law." They have said repeatedly that Cook did not commit mortgage fraud.
Will the committee be independent from the president?
No, the committee is made up of executive branch appointees who report to the president. They are tasked with weighing the evidence, and are required to hear Cook's point of view. But they are not impartial members of the judicial branch.
Does the committee need to find that Cook committed a crime?
No, it only needs to show that the president has cause to fire her. The Supreme Court didn't make a detailed determination of what constitutes cause, and that question will almost certainly be the subject of future litigation should Trump ultimately decide to remove her.
Roberts wrote in Trump v. Cook that a finding of cause depends "at least in part, on the seriousness of the alleged misconduct, and the extent of any nexus that may exist to the Governor's professional duties."
Could Cook's testimony expose her to criminal jeopardy?
Potentially. The order requires Cook to appear and allows Justice Department officials to question her, but it does not say whether her answers would be protected from use in a later criminal case.
The Fifth Amendment generally protects government employees from having statements that are compelled under threat of losing their jobs used against them in a criminal prosecution. But it is not yet clear whether Cook's testimony in this proceeding would qualify as legally compelled.
Her attorneys could therefore seek assurances about how her testimony would be used before she answers questions that could expose her to criminal liability. Invoking the Fifth Amendment or seeking immunity would not legally amount to an admission of guilt, though Trump could seek to portray it politically that way.
Will the committee have the final word on Cook's employment?
Almost certainly not. The committee will make a recommendation to Trump, but his decision may not be final either. The Supreme Court's ruling establishes that it is entitled to review the president's determination of cause. Should Trump proceed with firing Cook after the hearing, the decision will likely end up in front of the justices again, a process that could take months.
Will interest rates change as a result of the committee?
Cook is expected to participate in the Fed's upcoming vote on interest rates scheduled for Oct. 28. After the Supreme Court blocked Trump's earlier attempt to fire Cook, she remains as a member in good standing of the Fed.
Trump has not yet made another attempt to fire her, though the committee is tasked with making a recommendation on that question. She would likely continue to serve on the Fed during any court challenges after the committee process concludes.
What does the committee's creation mean for former Chair Jerome Powell or other Fed members?
Trump's decision to establish the committee has no immediate bearing on Powell's standing at the Fed. Powell ended his term as Fed chairman in May but can remain on as a voting member of the Fed's Board of Governors through January 2028.
Past Fed chairs have resigned their governorships once their term as the Fed's leader expired, but Powell said in March he wanted to stay on in order to see the end of a separate investigation against him "with transparency and finality."
That investigation concluded two weeks ago without any criminal charges, and the Department of Justice said it would not pursue the matter further. Powell hasn't spoken about the Cook matter since the Supreme Court's ruling.
The White House criticized a third Fed governor, Michael Barr, over his involvement as the Fed's top bank regulator in the failure of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. But the White House stopped short of calling for his resignation.
The Fed referred questions about the committee to Cook's attorneys. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has previously said the Fed would follow the Supreme Court's ruling.
– CNBC's Angela Greiling Keane , Kevin Breuninger , Erik Holm and Steve Liesman contributed to this report.

I grew up in Memphis, Tennessee, but my life began in China. That's where I was abandoned at just 3 days old, left on a sidewalk in Nanchang, Jiangxi Province.
For the longest time, I was told finding my birth family would be impossible. That part of my life became a closed chapter. But that changed after I had children of my own. Social media has made us all more connected, and suddenly what once felt impossible felt possible. I realized my story was worth sharing.
From a young age, I knew I was adopted. There was never an "a-ha" moment or a sit-down talk. It was simply something that was openly discussed in my family.
I do remember coming across documents stating I was an "officially abandoned child" though. Reading that, it fully sank in that my biological family had actually left me on a sidewalk. It was probably the first time I felt negative about being adopted.
My adoptive mom has never wavered in her belief that my biological family wanted me, but wanted a better life for me more. As a child, that belief cushioned me from my past. As an adult, I'm less convinced. I think they could have loved me, but it probably looked very different.
I was 14 months old when I was adopted from an orphanage. I was also very sick. My mom wasn't sure I would survive the first night she met me. I had pneumonia in both lungs and couldn't turn my very flat head because I'd spent so long lying untouched in a crib.
She told me the orphanage was extremely crowded and couldn't properly care for sick babies. She's convinced our match is what saved my life. I was finally cared for because a family was now waiting for me.
I have very happy memories of my childhood: fall festivals, Christmas lights with my mom, trips to the beach, Disney World, Thanksgiving gatherings where my cousins and I slept on the floor at my grandmother's house, and reading Harry Potter .
My grandmother would often say, "Of all the beautiful little girls, God brought you here all the way from China to be my precious angel." That was the general tone of my upbringing. My family made me feel loved, and I never felt like an outsider.
School wasn't always easy. I was teased for being adopted, but as everyone came to know about it, the jokes soon dried up. It wasn't until college, when I was surrounded by new people, that my Chinese identity became something I thought about more deeply.
As a child, I didn't seek out information about my biological family, but daydreamed about them. In my mind, my birth mother wore a yellow dress and I had a brother and sister.
For a long time, I treated my past as something fixed and untouchable. I believed the little information I had was all I would ever know, and actively searching for more felt frightening. I was in college before I even Googled my birth city for the first time. I was shocked to discover Nanchang looked modern and developed. Growing up, I'd been told it was rural and poor, that I was probably born in a hut and far better off in America. Looking back, it's almost laughable that it took me so long to look up my own birthplace. I simply never felt like I had permission to, even from myself.
At 7 years old, I had returned to China through a program for China's lost girls. We spent two weeks visiting Beijing, Shanghai, Xi'an and other cities. It was incredible, but I was still too young to fully process what the experience meant.
Today, my feelings about my abandonment are constantly evolving. As I've gotten older, I've become more heartbroken than at peace over what my biological mother may have endured and why she had to make the decision she did. Increasingly, I wonder whether I was abandoned or taken. Questions I once kept at arm's length now weigh heavily on me.
Part of that shift came after becoming a mother myself.
I gave birth to my daughter in 2021, and it changed my life in ways I still struggle to put into words. For the first time, I was holding a blood relative. I could hug someone who looked like me. The same happened when my son was born.
I hadn't spent much time around babies before having children, and holding them made me realize how impossibly small I must have been when my birth family let me go. I couldn't imagine being separated from my own children for a moment at 3 days old, let alone for a lifetime.
I think I grieved deeply during both postpartum periods while also experiencing overwhelming joy. Becoming a parent fundamentally changed how I understand my adoption. I no longer feel like only an adopted child with a loose connection to Chinese culture. I am a Chinese mother raising Chinese children.
That responsibility matters to me. My daughter is now in kindergarten, and we're learning together what being Chinese means. We read books, watch videos and talk about my adoption in age-appropriate ways. She knows I'm adopted, although she doesn't fully understand yet. Right now, I mostly want to teach her about China. I want our family to be familiar with holidays, traditions and foods that I am still discovering myself.
For most of my life, my past felt like a blank space that didn't belong to me, something I wasn't entitled to investigate. Sharing what little information I have now feels frightening but also empowering.
I'm in the early stages of searching for my birth family. Another woman adopted from the same orphanage and I have decided to search together. We're planning DNA tests and have already reached out to organizations including the Nanchang Project and Baobeihuijia in hopes of maximizing visibility once results come back.
There are so many questions I'd like answered. I'd love to know my family's history, where I come from and who my relatives are. If reconnecting wouldn't cause them distress, I'd like to understand what led to my abandonment and whether there was more to the story than the one-child policy. Mostly, though, I want to know their lives. Our similarities, our differences and our shared history.
I am admittedly ignorant of many of the details surrounding the one-child policy, largely by choice. It's very difficult to learn what birth mothers and daughters endured during that time while knowing my fate could have been very different. I was one of the lucky ones. I was adopted by parents who wanted and loved me, and have an extended family that welcomed me with kindness and care.
I often wonder what my life would have looked like had I remained in China. But given the circumstances of my abandonment, I don't believe it would have resembled the life I was fortunate enough to have. At best, I may have grown up unwanted; at worst, I could have faced some of the harsh realities many families endured during that time. As much as I grieve the loss and unanswered questions surrounding my beginnings, I would not choose a different outcome than the life I have today.
If I ever meet my biological parents, there's one thing I would want them to know above all else: "I hope my life is a reflection of what you wanted for me when you let me go." I can't change the past or fully understand what circumstances led to that decision, but I know it was not made without consequence. Whatever their reasons, they took a risk. I hope that through the life I've built, they would feel it was worthwhile.
Today, I'm a stay-at-home mom preparing to return to work. When I was younger, I dreamed of becoming a news producer for Good Morning America in New York City. I thought that would be the peak of my life.
That dream has passed, and with time I've come to understand something else: this is my peak. My family, my children, my life right now. Knowing that brings me comfort, and it also makes me excited for whatever comes next.

items.title: Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs
items.summary: Spreads have widened in the high-yield bond market, but that doesn't tell the whole story.
items.content:
Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs
Spreads in high yield recently widened to levels not seen since April.
Investors are demanding more compensation for taking on the riskiest credit.
Experts lay out the warning signs that could signal broader trouble ahead.
Ktsdesign/science Photo Library | Science Photo Library | Getty Images
Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.
High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.
The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis . Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.
Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.
The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.
Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.
It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.
Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.
"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.
He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.
That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.
"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."
While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.
In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.
"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.
'Generational opportunity' in bonds? Here's what to know
The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.
The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."
In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.
The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.
"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."
For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.
"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.
Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.
But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.
"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."
It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.
"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.
High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.
"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

Share ‘Anachronism’: Rubio’s civilisational rhetoric prompts pushback from Iran on social media
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks in Athens, Greece, on October 7, 2026, with the Acropolis in the background [Alexandros Vlachos/EPA]
Tehran, Iran – A speech by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio invoking memories of ancient Persia has been met with coldness or disdain across the Iranian political spectrum amid Washington’s ongoing war on Iran.
With the Acropolis in Athens as a backdrop, Rubio presented the United States, founded in the 18th century, as the inheritor of ancient Western civilisation running from Greece to Rome.

list 2 of 3 How US, Israel are waging a war on Iranian culture, education
list 3 of 3 Why has Iraq decided to ban online map service Waze?
During the speech, he argued that modern-day Western countries have lost their confidence, weakened their industries and militaries, and need renewed ambition and power in the future.
Referencing the ancient Greco-Persian Wars, he used the Persian destruction of Athens in 480 BC under King Xerxes I as an example of Western civilisation surviving an external enemy.
“The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines and razed the Acropolis to the ground,” Rubio said. He subsequently hailed the return of the Athenians and the construction of the Parthenon under Pericles.
The top US diplomat also directed his rhetoric against Iran’s current leaders, who have been in power since a 1979 Islamic revolution, calling them “fanatics” who run a “death cult” that wields martyrdom as a tool to achieve their political objectives.
“The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity,” Rubio claimed. He boasted that the choice of President Donald Trump’s administration was the “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.
The US and Iran have been at war since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28. While fighting between the two sides has subsided, the US has continued a naval blockade on Iran while shipping through the vital Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, and parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf both responded by invoking the Roman Emperor Valerian, who was captured alive by Persian King Shapur I’s forces in battle in 260 AD.
“Anyone who brings history into this must be prepared for its repetition,” Rezaei said.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused Rubio of flattening Greek, Roman, Christian and modern history.
It also accused the secretary of state of incorporating an “America First” narrative to legitimise a military escalation against Iran after a relative decrease in fighting since June when a now-defunct memorandum of understanding was agreed .
“It appears that the US has concluded it is better to justify its policy of coercion and force to the world under the beautiful neon lights of ‘philosophy of history’, instead of naked bullying that uses the language of cowboys,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said in a statement. He added that Rubio was resorting to “anachronism”, rehashing long buried historical events for modern-day legitimacy.
After the 2020 assassination of Qassem Soleimani, a commander in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Trump threatened to hit 52 Iranian sites “very hard”, including places “important to Iran & the Iranian culture”.
Since February, the US has been criticised for damaging Iranian historical and cultural sites during its bombing of Iran.
Culture Minister Reza Salehi-Amiri urged Western politicians to speak about Iran with a “language of respect” since “it is not an enemy created in a political speech but a living civilisation, a great nation and a lasting reality in world history” that dates back millennia.
Iranian historian Touraj Daryaei told local media on Friday that while Rubio’s account of the sack of Athens was true, he omitted an important fact cited by Greek historian Herodotus and others – a major motivation for the Persian attack was retaliation.
In 498 BC, Athens’ forces burned Sardis, a provincial Persian capital in western Anatolia. For Iranians who feel they were subject to an unprovoked attack by the US and Israel, this event could have modern-day relevance.
Shima, a 26-year-old resident of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that she did not appreciate Rubio’s attempt to use conflicts 2,500 years ago to muster support for the ongoing war with Iran.
“They want to continue the war, and they will say whatever they think will work in the moment,” she said.
During his January 2025 Senate confirmation hearing, Rubio had referred to Iranians as “the people of an ancient civilisation and culture with tremendous pride and advances who take great pride in their Persian heritage and identity”.
“I don’t know of any nation on Earth in which there’s a bigger difference between the people and those who govern them,” he said at the time. “In no way are the clerics who run the country representative of the people and its history and contributions it’s made to humanity.”
But the US war on Iran, its naval blockade of southern Iranian ports and isolating sanctions have not had the worst impact on Iran’s government and leaders but on Iranians themselves and have failed to change the behaviour of the government.
Trump’s comments on the potential “death of a civilisation” in Iran in case of a military escalation have instilled more pessimism among Iranians about the goals of the US war, which was initially cited as an attempt to free the people from their government.
Rubio speaks during a ceremony marking the renovation and opening of a new wing of the US embassy in Athens, Greece, on October 7, 2026 [Alexandros Vlachos/EPA] Most Iranians reacted negatively to Rubio’s latest speech although some members of the diaspora or others opposed to the Islamic Republic argued that the US secretary of state is against Iranian authorities, not an entire ancient civilisation.
Iranian state media were quick to slam Rubio for his remarks with the hardline Vatan-e Emrouz newspaper on Saturday publishing a front page image of Rubio in ancient Roman military attire and holding a shield and sword.
“Ancient war” read the headline. The newspaper claimed that Rubio was trying to “create historical-ideological backing for the US war against Iran”.
Vali Nasr, professor of international affairs and Middle East studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, DC, told Al Jazeera he believes Rubio’s aim was to define a common enemy for the US and Europe to rebuild their relations around.
“He decided that Iran, rather than Islam, which was previously viewed as the civilisational enemy, should play that role to bind the West together,” he said. “It also reflects US frustration that Europe has not played a major role in the war and seeks to paper over deep divisions between the US and Europe on Russia and Ukraine.”
Rubio delivered his speech as Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to sell diesel fuel to the US and global markets despite sanctions on Russia. The US president said the agreement would lower diesel prices, which have risen to record levels due to the Iran war. Nasr said Trump’s announcement and Rubio’s speech together could be a message by the administration that Iran and not Russia is the enemy the West should be focused on.
“I think whether this rhetoric would alienate Iranians was no more a concern than President [George W] Bush’s Islamophobia was a concern alienating Muslims,” Nasr told Al Jazeera. “However, it makes clear that Washington sees no difference between Iranians and Iran as a civilisation and the Islamic Republic.”

The International Gas Union Urges the European Commission to Use Pragmatism in Its Approach to Methane Emission Regulation
# IGU # International Gas Union # EuropeanCommission # Methane # Natural Gas # GAS # LNG
The International Gas Union (IGU) is calling on the European Commission (EC), as a matter of urgency, to postpone the importer obligations due in 2027 and 2028, for three years. This postponement would give the EC, the European Union (EU) Member States and Gas industry itself time to build a framework that enables a genuine and verifiable compliance, one based on reality and pragmatism rather than on ideology alone.
IGU’s position on the EU Methane Emissions Regulation (EUMR), together with that of other 16 international organisations, was made clear in a joint letter addressed to the EU Heads of State and Government and their respective Energy Ministers, ahead of the European Council meeting taking place on 15–16 October 2026.
IGU fully supports effective methane-abatement regulatory measures to drive transparent and credible data, monitoring, reporting and verification and we applaud our many members who are already committed to reducing their methane emissions by at least 30% and to operating with near-zero leaks by 2030.
IGU further welcomes the fact that over 50% of the oil & Gas industry is now committed to near-zero emissions, from less than 20% five years ago.
To effectively drive action, however, regulatory requirements should be designed around how natural gas is actually produced, transported and traded. Compliance methodologies need to be available before related obligations or penalties become enforceable, giving suppliers and buyers sufficiently clear rules and transition arrangements to make long-term commitments and ensure that natural gas continues to be delivered seamlessly to where it is needed the most.
Policymakers must avoid creating further uncertainty and energy insecurity by deterring investments in Gas supply and its infrastructure.

items.title: Trading Places: The U.S. and Europe on China and Russia - Council on Foreign Relations (CFR)
items.summary: Trading Places: The U.S. and Europe on China and Russia  Council on Foreign Relations (CFR)
items.content:
For years, the United States pressed Europe to join it in taking a harder position on defending itself against Russia and protecting itself against China. Europe resisted, insisting it could navigate a middle ground between the United States on one hand and Russia and China on the other.
How times have changed. Now, Europe is lecturing the United States on the threat Russia poses, while Washington is less committed to Ukraine’s defense and confronting Russian aggression. More interesting is that Europe appears to be taking steps to achieve escalation dominance in a potential trade war with China precisely at a time when the United States is emphasizing détente, strategic stability, and a decent peace with China.
From pushing European countries to increase their NATO defense spending—as U.S. presidents as far back as Dwight D. Eisenhower have done—to implementing sanctions and export controls against China, the United States has led from the front for years. In the meantime, Europe, and particularly Germany, pursued a strategy that left it overdependent on Russia for energy, China for markets, and the United States for security. Europe sought to prioritize economic ties and stability with these countries while leaving concerns about security and competition to the United States.
This week might mark the moment when the United States and Europe ultimately swapped positions. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after which point European security became a critically acute issue, the Europeans have increased their defense spending and switched to alternative sources of energy. At the same time, European leaders have beaten a path to the Oval Office to try to warn President Donald Trump of the dangers of accommodating Russian President Vladimir Putin. In turn, the Trump administration withdrew five thousand troops from Germany this spring, reduced overall U.S. force deployments to Europe to prewar levels, and cut direct military aid to Ukraine by 99 percent.
And, while the Trump administration raised tariffs on China to as high as 145 percent in the first half of 2025, Beijing’s subsequent threat to impose restrictions on exports of critical minerals, magnets, and related processing know-how resulted in the United States seeking to de-escalate and stabilize relations with China. This included delaying an arms sale to Taiwan, approving China’s access to advanced (but not the most advanced) semiconductor chips, reducing tariffs on select non-strategic goods, and choreographing a state visit for Chinese President Xi Jinping—which was long on respect and short on addressing conflicting interests.
This week, the Europeans showed that they may be taking a different tact. In a letter sent Monday to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron proposed that the European Union (EU) adopt a last-resort trade tool that would empower the European Commission to immediately cut off access to the EU’s single market in the face of China’s economic coercion, particularly on rare earth minerals. In the words of a senior German official, this new tool would operate as a “second-strike weapon” if China decides to exploit its chokepoints over rare earth minerals again, as it did last year. Rather than pull its punches, Europe seems to be warming up for a fight.
The proposal is, at this stage, just a proposal, but the language used by the two European leaders underscores a sea-change in Europe’s perspective. “The open and rules-based trade system is massively affected by weaponization of trade, systemic market-distorting practices, and global macroeconomic imbalances,” they write. They argue that the new trade instrument is needed to “give us the ability to counter cases where third countries deliberately seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions by political or economic means, leading to severe and systematic distortions of our internal market.” While they do not name any particular country—and while the United States could conceivably be a target—this tool was clearly designed with China in mind.
Macron and Merz’s letter amounts to a meaningful recognition by the drivers of European policy that China has the capacity and the will to wreak havoc on their economies through a combination of overcapacity, currency manipulation, and export controls. To Macron’s credit, the French have been beating this drum for some time now: for one, he was a strong backer of the EU’s tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs).
The reason that this announcement is noteworthy is that Germany has for years been a major impediment to Europe taking a more aggressive stance toward China on economic issues. Berlin has belatedly come to the conclusion that it has been the victim and target of Beijing’s concerted industrial policy, which is hollowing out Germany’s industrial base, eliminating manufacturing jobs, and undermining its economic independence, just as the country weans itself off Russian energy. To take just a few illustrative data points: Germany is losing ten thousand manufacturing jobs per month due to Chinese imports, and German auto giant Volkswagen plans to cut fifty thousand jobs and close four plants after Chinese EV makers flooded the market with better and cheaper cars. More broadly, Germany’s industrial sector eliminated more than 341,000 jobs in the past seven years, including the loss of one in seven auto jobs.
There are a few other takeaways from this announcement.
In August, I warned in an essay for Foreign Affairs that China’s export-dependent growth model is corroding the industrial base of its customers around the world, leading to protectionist politics and a reduction in global demand for Chinese goods that cannot be made up in the domestic Chinese market. That mismatch of oversupply and weak demand is kindling for an economic reckoning in China with potential implications for the broader global economy.
The instrument described by Macron and Merz is precisely the kind of economic weapon that, if deployed, would deprive China of the foreign consumers it needs to maintain its excess capacity-based, export-led growth strategy. In the best-case scenario, this proposal is Europe’s way of deterring China’s economic coercion and arming itself for negotiations, while remaining cognizant of the fact that one rarely negotiates a desirable outcome from a position of weakness. A trade deal that avoids a trade war is the ideal outcome, and a stronger Europe makes that more likely, not less.
When Germany cut itself off from Russian gas after the invasion of Ukraine, that was justified on obvious and explicit national security grounds: Germany would not fund the Russian war machine that it was spending billions of dollars to prevent from overrunning Ukraine. The pivot on China has national security ramifications but is driven by a more nuanced set of motivations. As reporting from the Financial Times confirms, Merz became convinced of the need to take on this stronger approach after seeing the profound pain inflicted on swaths of Germany’s industry. The hollowing out of Germany’s industrial base has, as in the United States and across Western Europe, fueled a rise in right-wing populist politics which has a distinct historical valence in Germany. The question for Merz, and the rest of Europe, is whether shifting positions like this is too little, too late.
Finally, it was difficult in the past to get Europe to cooperate with the United States in taking a firmer position vis-à-vis China. U.S. pleas were met with resistance and recalcitrance. Europe was reluctant to be dragged into what it viewed to be the United States’ obsession with competing with China and thought it could pursue a “third way.” This week’s announcement indicates that there is a new and growing appetite among our European allies for a more aggressive policy toward China, but it might be coming precisely at a time when the Trump administration, or least the president himself, appears to be reluctant to be confrontational. The risk is that the United States and Europe are again not entirely in sync.
The United States’ network of allies is one of its greatest geopolitical advantages. Everything from tariffs to export controls to investment screenings are likely to be more effective when like-minded countries join together. The Trump administration and future U.S. administrations will face a series of issues involving China—from Taiwan to artificial intelligence to critical minerals—where having these allies at our side, rather than on the sidelines, could prove invaluable. We shouldn’t get ahead of ourselves, but this proposal from Macron and Merz is a good sign that Europe is moving in the right direction. The question is, will the United States be there when they arrive?
Let me know what you think about Europe’s position on China and what this column should cover next by replying to [email protected] .

items.title: Adobe's Earnings Are on Track to Grow About Eightfold in a Decade. Why Has Its Stock Lagged the Market So Badly? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Adobe's Earnings Are on Track to Grow About Eightfold in a Decade. Why Has Its Stock Lagged the Market So Badly?</a
items.content:
A decade ago, shares of Adobe ( ADBE +0.51% ) closed at about $109. Today, they trade near $243 as I write. That's a rise of about 123%, enough to turn a $10,000 investment into about $22,300.
It seems OK until you compare it to the market. In the same period, $10,000 in an S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.59% ) index fund (with dividends reinvested) rose to around $42,100, a gain of about 321%.
And because Adobe doesn't pay a dividend, its stock price is the full return.
In other words, the creative software company has returned less than half as much as the broad market over the last decade. But its business kept growing all along. I think the gap boils down to how much investors were paying for Adobe's profits -- not the profits themselves.
In the first half of the decade, Adobe was one of the market's big winners. The stock closed at a record $688.37 in November 2021, more than six times its October 2016 price.
An S&P 500 index fund climbed around 138% over the same stretch.
Since then, the two have switched places. The index fund is up about 77% from that November 2021 close, but Adobe stock is about 65% off its peak.
Shares have dropped about 31% in 2026 alone, from roughly $350 when last year ended.
Much of this year's slide came as investors worried that artificial intelligence (AI) might disrupt software companies. AI agents could take over some of the work businesses pay for one seat at a time, and Adobe sells many of its subscriptions that way. By mid-January, Adobe was already among the S&P 500's worst performers of 2026 as software stocks sold off on these fears.
Showing how much Adobe grew under the surface, the company made $3.01 a share on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis in fiscal 2016. Five years later, that number was $12.48, and revenue had almost tripled, from $5.85 billion to $15.79 billion. For this fiscal year, management's target calls for adjusted earnings per share between $24.45 and $24.50, on around $26.6 billion in revenue. That's about eight times the fiscal 2016 level.
True, growth has slowed. Adjusted earnings per share compounded at around 33% a year from fiscal 2016 to fiscal 2021, versus about 14% a year since then if Adobe reaches this year's target.
Part of the fall in the stock's valuation was arguably deserved. But the slowdown hasn't become a decline. Revenue has grown 12% to 13% year over year in all three quarters Adobe has reported this fiscal year.
And in the fiscal third quarter of 2026 (the period ended Aug. 28, 2026), Adobe's adjusted earnings per share rose 15% over the year-ago quarter, to $6.13. Annualized recurring revenue from its AI-first products grew more than 150%.
The valuation is where the decade went. In October 2016, investors paid around 36 times Adobe's fiscal 2016 adjusted earnings per share. At the November 2021 high, the stock cost about 55 times its fiscal 2021 adjusted earnings.
Today's price is around 10 times this year's adjusted earnings target.
In other words, earnings per share are on track to grow about eightfold, while the price of each dollar of those earnings has fallen by about 73%. Together, these two numbers explain the stock's 123% gain.
I'd say a valuation of around 10 times adjusted earnings asks very little of Adobe. It's the sort of price the market tends to put on a business it expects to stall or shrink.
$94B Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Adobe's earnings per share are still growing at a double-digit rate. If its valuation multiple just stays around 10 times adjusted earnings, shares may climb about as fast as earnings per share from here.
Sure, the risk is that AI one day does to Adobe's growth what the market fears. Management's own target already calls for total annualized recurring revenue to climb 10.2% this year, a little slower than revenue. If that rate keeps falling toward the low single digits, today's price-to-earnings ratio might turn out to be fair.
In the end, I think the past decade says more about the price investors paid in 2021 than about the business. Back then, Adobe stock cost over 50 times adjusted earnings and needed almost everything to go right. Today it needs much less.
I'd consider buying Adobe stock today. But with AI's long-term impact on Adobe's customers still unknown, I'd start with a small position.
