Northern Oil and Gas recently saw its operating backdrop shift as a Gulf tanker attack disrupted flows through the Strait of Hormuz while hurricanes curtailed production in the Gulf of Mexico, pushing Brent above US$104 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate to US$92.
For Northern Oil and Gas, a non operated producer with a multi basin portfolio, this kind of supply shock highlights how exposure to benchmark pricing can reshape expected cash generation and capital allocation options even when its own assets remain physically unaffected.
We will now explore how the Northern Oil and Gas investment narrative is affected by tighter oil supply after the Strait of Hormuz disruption.
Spot 28 high quality undervalued stocks that could also benefit when shocks to supply push benchmark prices higher, alongside Northern Oil and Gas and its energy sector peers.
To own Northern Oil and Gas, you need to be comfortable with a non operated, multi basin model that leans heavily on operators to keep volumes steady while management focuses on capital allocation. The recent oil price spike after the Strait of Hormuz disruption mostly feeds into near term cash flow sensitivity, rather than changing that core thesis.
The key short term swing factor remains how effectively Northern Oil and Gas converts this pricing backdrop into free cash flow while carrying higher cost notes and a dividend that is not well covered. The biggest risk still sits in earnings optics, with potential non cash impairments, hedge marks and rising expenses offsetting any benefit from stronger realized prices.
There have been no fresh company announcements directly tied to the Gulf tanker attack or hurricane related production halts. This means the recent move in Northern Oil and Gas is being interpreted mainly through its existing playbook. The non operated, multi basin footprint and tilt toward longer life assets like Utica gas and Duvernay oil already framed how it responds to commodity swings.
In that context, the most relevant ongoing theme is management’s focus on acquisitions that add lower decline inventory while keeping dividends and buybacks covered by free cash flow. Energy price spikes can give more room to fund that plan. However, higher leverage and interest costs still sit in the background as constraints that investors need to watch closely.

items.content:
Nobel peace prize winner Navi Pillay jokes about sharing award with Donald Trump – video
ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza .
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X , adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement , the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize , the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.
Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.
The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.
The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.
“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.
Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa , home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment , she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

items.title: 'Cockroach' group leaders among hundreds detained in Delhi protest
items.summary: Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration.
items.content:
Image caption, Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions
By Matt Spivey ,  Geeta Pandey   and   Azadeh Moshiri
Hundreds of protesters have been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over electoral reforms.
The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke, who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches", was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi.
Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead.
Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital.
The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.
It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.
Under Kumar's leadership, India's election commission has undertaken a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - it said this was a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.
But in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.
The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.
The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.
Before arriving in Delhi, the CJP's founder Dipke said: "If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken."
He and and two other leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained on their flight from Mumbai on Saturday.
The group claimed the three men have been taken to an undisclosed location. Delhi Police have not commented.
Figure caption, 'Cockroach' leaders say they have been detained ahead of march
Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's new designated leader while the others are in detention, released a video telling protesters that "if Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar".
Student activist Neha Bora, who had also been detained by Delhi Police, urged demonstrators to "hold the line".
The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks.
Announcements could be heard across the city, asking people to co-operate with the police.
One protester, Sabika Muzaffar, told the BBC she and her mother expected to be detained.
"On the way to the protest site, instead of reciting hymns and verses as we usually do, my mother and I were rote learning our lawyer's number," she said.
She said that showing up to protest was "her way of defending the country and its democracy".
A few minutes after Muzaffar spoke to the BBC she was taken away by police.
Several trains to and from major Delhi stations had been cancelled and dozens of metro stations were closed from Friday night.
Buses packed with detained protesters were seen being driven away from the protest site.
Image caption, Detained protesters were driven away from the site in police buses
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.
Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"
The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.
In July, Dipke watched from the stage as the five-week-long protest ended in celebration after the resignation of India's education minister.

items.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
items.summary: After four years, a Ukrainian man is set to stand trial in Hamburg accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream pipelines.
items.content:
Image caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022
By Sarah Rainsford Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent
Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.
Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.
After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.
Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".
Both he and his country have denied any involvement.
Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.
Image caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor
It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.
There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.
Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.
They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.
Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.
As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.
Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.
But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.
The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.
In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.
That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.
He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.
But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.
Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.
By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.
Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.
None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.
But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them.
"Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."
Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.
That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.
Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution.
"Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.
The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.
Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence.
"At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.
Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".
Image caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia
Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.
He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.
Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.
Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.
Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.
In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".
As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."
The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.
After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.
It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.
It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.
When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".
This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further.
"I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.
He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe.
"Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."
Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.
Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.
He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.
His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.
And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.
His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.
I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.

items.content:
From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments
Dollar General, BJ's Wholesale Club, Lululemon and Under Armour have said in earnings calls that they have already cut or plan to cut assortments.
Analysts said that after trimming product lines, brands may focus on raising prices to get back to healthy growth.
Box retailers can offer thousands of individual brands, so product cuts can help streamline assortments and stabilize their businesses.
Trimming assortments comes with challenges, as retailers risk losing customers and have to answer to investors as their revenue base shrinks in the short term.
Why retail companies are taking products off shelves
Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets.
As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs.
In March, Dollar General said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ's Wholesale Club said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs . In September, Lululemon said it cut North America SKUs by 15%.
Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make.
A person shops at Macy's in Herald Square, in New York, June 3, 2026.
When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don't end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems.
"If you have zero discounting, you're not taking enough fashion risk," said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. "But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly."
Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns.
Under Armour's operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue.
"Today, we're managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy," said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. "We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price."
Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power.
A clearance rack in a Lululemon store in New York, Oct. 7, 2026.
Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years.
"Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things," said Siegel. "Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer."
Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand.
Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level.
"It's a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception," said Siegel.
He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026.
Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is "rebalancing" its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June.
A sale sign is displayed on the soft drinks aisle at a Dollar General discount store in Inglewood, California, Sept. 29, 2026.
For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ's, cutting down the assortment doesn't necessarily give them the ability to raise prices.
Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business.
"When you shrink a box ... and say, I'm going to focus more on curation, you're getting smaller, but you're trying to reestablish why someone's walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn't necessarily help your bottom line as much," said Siegel.
BJ's CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren't previously offered.
"That is sourcing sales growth as well and sort of giving us the formula where we can cut SKUs, and see sales go up, and see margin dollars go up," Eddy said on the company's fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August.
A BJ's Wholesale Club store in Miami, Florida, Nov. 21, 2025.
In June 2025, Dollar General said the elimination of 1,000 SKUs from the previous year opened up more shelf space for its best-selling products and added to its top line. By March 2026, the company said, it had reduced up to 1,500 SKUs, providing benefits to the overall supply chain.
"Being more productive there means getting product to the shelf faster and being there for the consumer with the right amount of items and products that she's looking for as quickly as we possibly can," Dollar General CEO Todd Vasos said in the company's fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August. "As we go forward, the team is looking at continued SKU rationalization, albeit probably more surgical in nature."
Successfully slashing products from shelves is difficult in practice.
Box stores risk losing customers to competitors that offer the products they scrapped. BJ's, for instance, acknowledged that a previous attempt to cut SKUs was unsuccessful.
"We just cut SKUs which cut sales, and then we added some SKUs back and so really what we're doing now is removing unnecessary choice," Eddy said on the company's earnings call in August. "Think about in traditional soda, we don't carry cans and one-liters and two-liters of the same product anymore."
Meanwhile, publicly traded brands that acknowledge sales need to decline in order for the business to grow still have answers to investors in the near term.
"It's hard for a company ever to say we need to shrink anything, but it's dramatically harder to say we need to shrink revenues," said Siegel. "Frequently we find that brands hit a peak, a healthy peak, extend past the peak by forcing it and then find their way back down pretty harshly."

items.content:
Fired OpenAI employees raise safety concerns The three fired workers say OpenAI punished them for being outspoken about safety. The company disputes the claims and says they were fired over mishandling sensitive information.
Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety
Three employees recently fired by OpenAI allege the company punished them for being outspoken about safety. OpenAI disputes the claims and says they were dismissed for mishandling sensitive information.
Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology .
The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions
The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.
OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.
Anthropic and OpenAI CEOs call for AI development to slow down, OpenAI to delay IPO
The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.
The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.
In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.
This is how evaluators test if an AI model is safe, and what they're checking for
As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators , who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.
The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.
In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.
In a statement OpenAI posted on X , the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."
The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.
"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.
"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.
He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.
A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X , echoing Balesni's concerns.
The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.
In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.
Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.
Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.
"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."
OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.
OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.
In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.
"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

items.title: How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen - CNN
items.summary: How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen  CNN
items.content:
A pro-Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighter fires a vehicle-mounted weapon during what government forces say was an advance against the Iran-backed Houthis, near Dhubab, Taiz Governorate, Yemen, in this still image taken from video released on Monday.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman wanted to make his kingdom a magnet for investment , tourism and the world’s biggest sporting events. Now drones and missiles launched from Yemen are slamming into Saudi cities, drawing the kingdom deeper into the regional turmoil he hoped to leave behind.
The civil war in Yemen erupted once again this summer and significantly intensified last month, breaking years of relative calm. Saudi Arabia has for 11 years tried to contain the conflict on its southern border through military force and diplomacy – first waging war with the Iran-allied Houthi group, then pursuing peace talks with them and restoring diplomatic talks with their backer, Iran.
Despite the efforts, a series of miscalculations has left Riyadh exposed to further conflict in Yemen, experts say. Saudi Arabia’s ended its longstanding partnership with the UAE late last year over its backing of a rival force in Yemen, misjudged President Donald Trump’s willingness to back it if it needed support, and struggled to organize disintegrated armed factions fighting the Houthis in Yemen.
Now, Riyadh is trying to regain its footing by supporting its Yemeni partners in yet another campaign against the Houthis, an operation named “Yemen’s Dawn.”
Prince Mohammed’s ambitions to transform his kingdom have already faced several challenges since his rise to power more than a decade ago. Today, they’re coming under further strain as multi-front attacks on oil infrastructure cut into exports, major projects are canceled, and the kingdom is pulled into a war with no clear way out.
At least three people, including a Saudi pilot, were killed this week after Houthi forces struck several airports in the kingdom, according to Saudi Arabia. Regional turmoil has forced the suspension of star-studded film festivals, award shows, and music concerts this year. Meanwhile, the kingdom’s flagship financial conference, which is expected to draw high-profile business leaders at the end of October, is coming under pressure amid the strikes.
“They just needed the conflict to stay (as) far away from them as possible without the Houthis disrupting their transformation plans,” Michael Ratney, the former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told CNN. “Now they find themselves in the middle of it.”
Damaged military vehicles, reportedly sent by the United Arab Emirates to support Southern Transitional Council (STC) separatist forces, following an air strike carried out by the Saudi-led coalition in the port of Mukalla, southern Yemen, on December 30.
When Saudi warplanes struck a shipment of military vehicles sent to Yemen by the UAE last year, a decade-old alliance between two nations fighting Iran’s influence in Yemen shattered, leaving the kingdom to contend with the crisis alone after Abu Dhabi withdrew its forces. The break with the UAE shocked the region. Saudi Arabia launched a rare media campaign against its neighbor, accusing it of fueling instability in Sudan and Yemen. Saudi commentators publicly cast the UAE as a younger sibling rebelling against a wiser one.
Saudi Arabia is the “head and body” on which regional stability rests, wrote prominent Saudi journalist Dawood Al-Shirian in January. “If (Saudi Arabia) stumbles, the entire system is disrupted and the Gulf scatters.”
As Riyadh pressed for dominance in the Gulf, the ground shifted in Yemen. The four-year ceasefire with the Houthis was already fragile, and the rapid UAE withdrawal as demanded by Riyadh left thousands of fighters who had spent a decade under Abu Dhabi’s command disoriented by Riyadh’s strategy.
Fighters allied with the UAE say Abu Dhabi’s departure left a power vacuum the Saudis didn’t fill.
“There wasn’t a proper transition when the Emiratis left,” a southern Yemeni official, who asked to remain anonymous to speak freely to CNN, said. “It was frightening how different things became. The Emiratis’ command and control was very efficient, and the Saudis did not replace this efficiency.”
CNN reached out to the Saudi government for comment on whether the forces fighting the Houthis on the ground received enough support and whether there was a proper transition.
Protesters brandish billboards depicting the late Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, flags of Yemen and Iran, and weapons as they take part in a rally held to condemn the US-Israel attacks on Iran that killed Khamenei, in Sana'a, Yemen, on March 1.
Eight weeks after the UAE withdrawal, the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, killing supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The moves sparked a conflict that has plunged the region into unprecedented turmoil and placed Washington’s allies, including Saudi Arabia, in Iran’s crosshairs.
The timing was unfortunate for Saudi Arabia, several experts say. After contending with the UAE-backed separatist push in Yemen, the US and Israel triggered a regional war. And despite years of trying to stop the war from breaking out in Yemen, the pressure Trump imposed on Iran was expected to eventually trigger a Houthi push on the kingdom.
“The Saudis had to respond after being attacked by an enemy force on their territory… so there was always going to be a response,” Ratney, the former US ambassador, said.
Even as Iranian missiles struck the kingdom from the east, Saudi attention focused on the south. The Houthis, still formally in a truce with Riyadh, appeared unwilling to aid their Iranian partners. Tehran instead drew the Saudis in.
In July, Iran sent a commercial plane to carry a Houthi delegation to Khamenei’s funeral in Tehran, defying a Saudi air blockade of Yemen. Riyadh struck the Houthi-held airport in Sanaa to prevent the plane from landing. The rebel group retaliated by declaring the truce dead and announced a naval blockade on Saudi ships. It also started a lightning offensive down Yemen’s coast, seizing strategic territory at the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the largest escalation since 2022.
A satellite image shows the Saudi Arabia East-West pipeline, located across the Arabian Peninsula, after a strike on September 11.
The Houthis attacked Saudi oil facilities and pipelines, disrupting crude supplies and sending prices sharply higher. Saudi forces answered with hundreds of airstrikes.
“The Saudis have made several mistakes and failures,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen with the International Crisis Group think tank, told CNN, noting that Riyadh hadn’t prepared for a Houthi offensive and lacked coordination with allied Yemeni forces it inherited from the UAE.
“The areas they’ve lost created morale issues with their allies and now it’s a big challenge for the Saudis as the Houthis have more advanced weaponry which managed to reach several cities in Saudi Arabia,” he said.
US President Donald J. Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman attend a bilateral meeting at the Saudi Royal Court in Riyadh, on May 13, 2025.
Another miscalculation by Saudi Arabia was its reliance on continued American support, experts say. Despite signing a new defense pact with Washington last year and being designated a Major Non-NATO Ally by the US, Riyadh has been disappointed by what it sees as waning US commitment to its security.
Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month, urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but Trump declined to intervene. Washington instead met the Houthis in Oman, seeking to protect its own ceasefire with the group, which made it clear that its war was with Saudi Arabia alone, thus allowing US vessels to traverse the Red Sea freely.
For a military that has built its “entire worldview” around partnering with the US, the Saudis are realizing how unpredictable Trump is, said Ratney.
“It was never their concept or the structure of their military to fight these wars by themselves,” he said. “Under a normal US presidency, if something like this happens, we would’ve helped our partner in what would’ve been a rational and considered process.
“Now we don’t have that process, and it ultimately comes down to: what does Trump think? And the Saudis probably feel exposed as a result,” he added.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, left, met Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, in Cairo, Egypt, on September 15.
Saudi Arabia has since looked elsewhere. Last month, Prince Mohammed flew to Egypt to meet President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, then invited UAE Vice President Sheik Mansour bin Zayed to Riyadh a few weeks later to discuss regional developments. France agreed to deploy defense assets, including military personnel. Britain said it would send an aircraft to help refuel Saudi jets. More than 100 American military advisers are on the ground providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly established joint forces command.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed on Monday to “activate collective deterrence measures” under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement after an emergency meeting in Riyadh. The pact, set up earlier this year, is meant to coordinate defense and security cooperation among the three. Forces loyal to the UAE also appear to be taking part in the offensive, a sign of at least a partial thaw between the kingdom and the UAE.
Forces loyal to Yemen's Saudi-backed government ride in pick-up trucks along a road in the Hays district, south of Hodeidah on September 5.
But experts warn that outside support and early gains by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government will not settle the conflict. Infighting remains common among the factions, and there is still no clear political end state.
A sustained push against Iranian-backed forces, analysts say, would require organization, regional backing, funding, and logistics that the current coalition has not yet shown it can sustain.
“They need to unify their command centers, they need to resolve the issues they have between the various factions within the group,” Hisham Al Omeisy, a senior Yemen adviser for the European Institute of Peace told CNN’s Becky Anderson. “Territorial gains they’ve made would mean nothing if the (Saudi-backed) Yemeni government cannot maintain control over those areas.”
Many experts said however that the fighting in Yemen is connected to the US war in Iran, and as long as the conflict between Washington and Tehran is ongoing, the Iranians will continue having a powerful incentive to watch the Houthis disrupt Saudi Arabia.
Gulf states could manage to secure a separate diplomatic solution with Iran, analysts say, or escalate their military strikes to eliminate Houthi leadership.
“Neither of those scenarios fix the conflict in Yemen in any near term,” Ratney said. “The Saudis will have to just figure out an imperfect path ahead.”

United Nations Special Envoy to Yemen Hans Grundberg says that the country has slid back into “full-scale war” as fighting between the Houthis and internationally recognised government forces continues.
During a meeting at the UN Security Council on Friday to discuss the situation in Yemen, Grundberg said civilians, including women and children, were bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.

“Ongoing instability in the Middle East continues to impact dynamics in Yemen, while developments in Yemen, in turn, reverberate across the region,” he said.
“Regional security, freedom of navigation and the protection of international trade are legitimate concerns that must be addressed. International engagement on Yemen must also be grounded in the realities of Yemen and the needs and aspirations of its people,” Grundberg added.
The envoy stressed that “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now.”
“Ultimately, gains on the battlefield cannot substitute for the negotiations that will be required to settle the conflict,” he said, urging Security Council members to collectively support mediation efforts.
According to the UN, at least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others have been injured since August, with children bearing a disproportionate toll during the ongoing clashes.
The UN representative for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Abdullah Ali Fadhel al-Saadi, told the Security Council that the threat from the Houthis was no longer an “internal Yemeni affair”.
Al-Saadi called on the council to take “decisive, practical measures” to reduce the flow of funding, weapons and technology to the Iranian-backed group and also strengthen cooperation with the Yemeni government.
He thanked Riyadh, which supports the government, for “standing beside the Yemeni people and their government, and for their continued support to state institutions and our economy”.
This comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continue, with the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority reporting on Friday that the King Khalid International Airport, north of Riyadh, was subjected to two attacks on Thursday, in which three Saudi citizens were killed.
Gulf states and European countries have condemned the attack on the airport, with Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs calling it “unacceptable”.
During the council meeting, Saudi Arabia’s UN representative, Abdulaziz al-Wasil, said the UN body must address the “dangerous escalation” ongoing in Yemen.
“These rapid developments in Yemen and the continued escalation by the terrorist Houthi militias must be addressed by the Council,” al-Wasil said.
Al-Wasil added that Riyadh will “not allow Yemen to be turned into a staging ground for threats to its security or to the freedom of navigation”.

Letter to the editor: Beware of right to natural gas question in Amendment 82
The upcoming November Colorado state ballot will have a dangerous and deceptive initiative on it, Amendment 82, "Right to Natural Gas", which may seem harmless, but it's not. It's a blatant attempt by the fossil fuel industry to put barriers into our state constitution to make it difficult, if not impossible, to prevent developers and utilities from installing methane gas supplies to new developments. It's sparsely worded on purpose. A recent example of this is a development in Aurora with 25,000 homes, to which Xcel was requesting last year a natural gas supply line (5 miles long, costing $23 million), which would have caused higher bills for all Xcel customers to cover the cost, while allowing 25,000 additional homes to spew yet more carbon with equipment that will be obsolete in the near future.
At this point, every pound of carbon emitted matters, and the sooner we get off methane gas and other fossil fuels, and construct only all-electric buildings powered with renewable energy, the better. However, Amendment 82 is about more than that. It's about whether we should let monopoly utilities and corporate polluters write themselves into our constitution permanently. The reality is that renewables are less profitable than fossil fuels, not to us homeowners, but to traditional energy companies, which is why we can expect gas and big oil to fight this transition at every turn. No pollution in the constitution: Vote no on Amendment 82!
